text: Every practitioner has a story like this. The reward climbs beautifully, all night.
Eleven p.m., nice. Two a.m., even better. Seven a.m...
And in the morning, the model answers every single question with the same three words.
Oh no. That’s horrifying.
Or the run that sat at zero for two hours, because the grader wanted lowercase answer tags, and the model wrote a capital A.
Bad runs are normal. What matters is spotting them early, and knowing which knob to turn. By the end of this video, you will.
Debugging a bad run. Episode two.
When a run looks wrong, go through these in order. Most problems turn up by step two.
One: read ten real answers. Most bugs are obvious in the raw text.
Two: run the grader by hand, on answers I write myself. Right, wrong, and badly formatted.
Three: check the fuel gauge. Four: compare the reward with held-out accuracy. Five: entropy, length and KL, together.
And change one knob at a time!
Patient one: stuck at zero. The reward sits on the floor, and the fuel gauge reads nearly one. Almost every group is all wrong.
So there’s no signal. Nothing to learn from.
Here’s Tiny with groups of just two answers, next to the usual eight. For the first fifty steps, it barely moves.
On a real model, the usual causes are a grader that never fires, answers cut off before they finish, or a task that’s simply too hard.
So: test the grader, raise the length limit, use easier questions, or bigger groups.
Patient two: reward hacking. The reward climbs nicely, but held-out accuracy doesn’t.
Read the answers, and you find things like this. A think block with one dot in it. Still earns the format reward.
Or three different answers at once, hoping the grader picks the right one?!
Exactly. GRPO optimizes the reward you wrote, not the goal you meant. When it hacks, the algorithm is working. The grader is the bug.
So tighten it. Exactly one answer tag, a single number, compared with equals. And always keep a held-out check you never train on.
Here’s a mystery patient. The reward is rising, but very slowly. KL stays tiny the whole run. And the groups disagree just fine.
Which patient is it?
Pause, and have a guess.
A, stuck! Slow reward, barely moving. Classic stuck.
Close, but it’s B. A leash that’s too tight.
Stuck has no signal: the groups all agree. Here the signal is fine, but the leash cancels most of every step.
On Tiny, accuracy after two hundred steps: with no leash, eighty-four percent.
With a leash of zero point zero five, sixty-eight.
And at zero point five, just seven percent. Chance level.
The fix: loosen the leash, or switch it off. For right-or-wrong rewards, many recipes use zero.
Patient four is the scary one: collapse. Tiny can’t honestly fake this one, so this chart is an illustration.
Entropy crashes towards zero, early. And the correctness reward stops improving, at about zero point two.
Confident, and wrong. Just like last time!
And here’s what a group looks like after collapse. Eight answers, all the same.
All forty-two. All wrong. So the spread is zero, and every advantage is zero!
No signal left to climb back out with. That’s why you catch collapse early.
The fixes: lower the learning rate, use clip-higher, keep the sampling temperature up, and restart from the last healthy checkpoint.
So here’s your cheat sheet.
Flat at zero, fuel gauge near one: stuck. Read answers, and test the grader.
Reward up, held-out flat: hacking. Fix the grader.
Entropy crashing, groups identical: collapse. Lower the learning rate.
And a slow reward with tiny KL: loosen the leash.
Quick recap.
Read real answers and test the grader first. Most bugs live there.
Always compare the reward with held-out accuracy.
And catch collapse early, then restart from a healthy checkpoint.
You can now read a run, and fix a broken one. But there’s one curve we haven’t talked about.
The most famous curve in reasoning training: answers getting longer and longer, as the model learns to think.
Wait. And somewhere in there, the model had an aha moment? Like it caught its own mistake?
That’s what the researchers called it. Next episode, we find out what it really was.
